title: My Team Answered Leads in 2 Minutes. We Were Still Dropping Them.
description: What happened when I measured lead follow-up in my own cleaning company: fast first replies, then missed callbacks, unsent prices and no voicemails. Here is the AI setup that catches them now.
author: Roy Banwell
content:
When I first measured how my cleaning company handles leads, I expected to find a speed problem. I didn't. My team reached most new leads within a couple of minutes. The problems were all after that first touch, and no rule I wrote caught them, because every dropped lead was a case nobody had thought of. This post is the short version of what I found and what I built. The full system, step by step, is in the free AI Lead Follow-Up Playbook.

The short answer

Speed to the first reply is table stakes, and most teams already do it. The leads you lose are the ones where somebody owes the customer something (a callback, a price, a reply) and it quietly never happens. Rules can't catch those reliably. An AI that reads each whole conversation and says what's owed, and by when, can.

What I found when I turned the system on

  • Zero voicemails in 26 calls on the first day. 23 rang out and 3 hung up at the beep. The team called fast and never left a message.
  • Four customers had been waiting 10 to 66 hours for a reply to a text they had sent us.
  • The main email inbox was unwatched. Over about four weeks, 16 of 209 emails were new customers asking for a quote, and five had never had a reply.
  • The text drip wasn't firing. Of 24 leads we checked who never answered us, 20 had never received a single automated text. The sequence existed; the tag that started it wasn't being added.

Across 935 real leads over two months, the ones who got a real phone conversation were about three times as likely to book as the ones who never did. And the top reasons leads were lost were never being reached (29% of lost leads) and going silent after talking to us (26%). Both are follow-up problems. The full numbers are in the lead response benchmark.

Why rules weren't enough

I started with rules: touch every lead three times on day one, remind the person on shift every two hours, and so on. Each time I found a dropped lead, I added a rule. A customer asked for a call at 10:18, and our first reminder went out at 11:41 because of the two-hour pacing. Someone promised a price and never sent it. A customer said "no need to follow up" and the rules kept pinging. Two callbacks were missed because the conversations were in Spanish.

The rules also got loud. At the worst point, one day had 208 messages in the lead channel, 54 leads raised 235 times, and one lead reminded 13 times. My team told me they were overwhelmed.

What fixed it: an AI that asks "what do we owe them?"

After every new message or call, an AI reads the whole conversation: the last 25 messages, every call transcript, and the team's notes. It gives one answer: is anything owed, and if so, is it a call, a price, a reply or a follow-up, and by when. Only then does anyone get pinged.

I ran it silently next to the old rules first. In three days it found 81 leads where something was owed and the rules hadn't noticed. In a later two-day head-to-head, it sent 3 wrong pings (plus one borderline) and missed nothing. The old rules sent about 20 noise pings and missed the callback, the promised price and the two Spanish callbacks.

The guardrails that matter

  • Silence is never a no. A customer who went quiet or is checking with a spouse is still a prospect. That rule is enforced in code, not just in the prompt.
  • Our "I'll get back to you" is a debt. A price we promised is owed within 30 minutes.
  • Any touch after a ping ends it until the customer writes again. No more pinging someone who already called.
  • The owner only hears about real misses, and each one says what to do: a call time passed 30+ minutes ago, a customer waiting 60+ minutes, a price owed 2+ hours, or a new lead not called in 30 minutes.

What I would build first

  1. An automatic first reply on every lead source, including email and after-hours forms.
  2. A junk filter, so vendors and job applicants never reach your team.
  3. A 15-minute nudge in your team chat for any lead nobody has touched.
  4. The AI reader, run silently first, then driving the reminders.

The AI Lead Follow-Up Playbook covers all seven automations, the exact thresholds, what to measure and a three-week build order. It's free.

Frequently Asked Questions

Isn't fast speed to lead enough?

No. In my company the first reply was already fast, a median of about 2 minutes on shift. The losses came after the first touch: callbacks that didn't happen, prices that weren't sent, replies that sat for hours, and calls with no voicemail.

Can't I just write rules in my CRM for follow-up?

You should start there, and rules handle the predictable parts well (the first reply, the drip). But every dropped lead I found was a situation no rule covered. An AI reading the whole conversation catches those, and in my test it was both quieter and more accurate than the rules.

Does an AI follow-up system text customers on its own?

Mostly not. The automatic texts are normal CRM messages and drips. The one place AI writes to customers is email: it replies to new customers in our inbox with the estimate link and asks for a phone number. Everywhere else, the AI reads conversations and tells a person what is owed. My team still does the selling.

How do I stop a follow-up bot from overwhelming my team?

End a reminder as soon as anyone touches the lead, cap tags at a few per hour per person, read the team's thread notes ("bad lead", "booked") as a stop, and escalate to the owner only for specific misses.
